newsitem.title: LIBYA: Libya marks the 11th anniversary of U.S. air raids.
newsitem.headline: Libya marks the 11th anniversary of U.S. air raids.

text.p: Libya marked on Monday the 11th anniversary of U.S. air raids on Tripoli and Benghazi by proclaiming a national day of mourning across the country.

An official statement said postal and telecommunications links between Libya and the rest of the world were cut and shipping and internal air flights were halted. Traffic stopped throughout the country and petrol was not on sale.
Libyan radio said people wore black clothes or put black signs on their garments and on cars and buses. Black banners were also displayed in streets and placed on buildings as a sign of mourning.
The government asked Libyan nationals not to travel to the United States and Britain on this day and travel agencies not to issue tickets to these destinations.

On April 15, 1986, U.S. warplanes bombed targets in Tripoli and Benghazi. Libya said some 40 people were killed including a girl adopted by Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi whose house in the Azizia barracks in Tripoli was destroyed during the raids.
Washington said the raids were in response to an explosion at a Berlin discotheque in which two Americans were killed. The United States blamed Libya but Tripoli denied the charge.
"We keep our right to retaliate to the aggression," the daily Azzahf al-Akhdhar (The Green Advance) which is run by the pro-Gaddafi Revolutionary Committees wrote in an editorial on Monday.

Among participants in a symposium held in Libya to mark the raids was British Labour MP for Liverpool Riverside Robert Parry who expressed hopes that the Labour party would change Britain's policy towards Libya if it won the forthcoming elections.

"I hope that the return of a new Labour government will adopt this cause of lifting sanctions," Parry told the symposium called "International Spring Festival for Peace and Freedom", which opened on Sunday night.

Tripoli has been under U.N. sanctions, including an air embargo to and from Libya, since April 1992 for refusing to extradite two Libyans wanted in the United States and Britain in connection with the bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988 in which 270 people were killed.
